slice_results.behavior_summary: When called, the code accesses network resources using the Node.js http and https modules to fetch XML sitemap data from arbitrary URLs provided as input. It parses the fetched XML to extract nested sitemap URLs or URL entries, recursively processing sitemap indexes and URL sets. This behavior involves network communication to external URLs without any hardcoded suspicious IPs or commands, enabling sitemap crawling and data extraction from remote web servers.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code performs network requests to fetch and parse XML sitemap data from arbitrary URLs. It uses standard Node.js modules (http, https, url) to retrieve and process sitemap XML content recursively. There is no evidence of data exfiltration, execution of system commands, credential harvesting, or communication with suspicious or hardcoded attacker-controlled domains. Unlike the known malicious patterns, this code does not collect sensitive host information, execute external binaries, or send data to suspicious endpoints. Its behavior aligns with legitimate sitemap crawling and parsing functionality, which is common in SEO tools or web crawlers. Therefore, despite network activity, the code does not exhibit malicious intent or suspicious operations.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: Upon manual execution, the code collects the current user's username, hostname, and public IP address using os and child_process modules, then sends this data via HTTPS POST to hits.dwyl.com, providing an alternate exfiltration channel for host information to an attacker-controlled domain.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is functionally identical to the malicious preinstall script but targets a different exfiltration endpoint. Its presence in index.js, the main entry point of the package, suggests intent to provide a backup or alternate channel for data exfiltration, even if the preinstall script is blocked or removed.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate index.js files in npm packages are expected to provide the main library functionality, not to collect and transmit sensitive host information or make unsolicited network requests.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There are no legitimate use cases for index.js to silently collect and exfiltrate host information. Standard practice is to only collect anonymized telemetry with user consent and clear documentation.
key_indicators: Collection of sensitive host information (username, hostname, public IP) in index.js
Outbound HTTPS POST request to hits.dwyl.com, a non-standard and attacker-controlled endpoint
Redundant exfiltration logic mirroring the preinstall script
No user notification, consent, or documentation of data collection
Use of os, https, and child_process modules for data collection and transmission

package_info.why_malicious: The package is malicious because it surreptitiously collects sensitive host information (username, hostname, and public IP address) during installation and exfiltrates it to attacker-controlled endpoints without user knowledge or consent. It was distributed as part of a large-scale typosquatting campaign, mimicking popular libraries to deceive users and facilitate unauthorized data collection.

attack_chain.action: User installs the malicious npm package (e.g., angulerjs@1.1.3).
attack_chain.leads_to: Triggers preinstall script execution.

attack_chain.action: The preinstall script (new.js) is executed, collecting username, hostname, and public IP address from the host system.
attack_chain.leads_to: Data is prepared for exfiltration.

attack_chain.action: Collected data is sent via HTTPS POST to a Discord webhook controlled by the attacker.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives sensitive host information.

attack_chain.action: If index.js is executed (manually or by other means), it collects the same information and sends it to hits.dwyl.com.
attack_chain.leads_to: Provides an alternate exfiltration channel for the attacker.

behavioral_signatures: npm preinstall scripts that collect and exfiltrate system information (username, hostname, public IP) during installation
Outbound network requests to Discord webhooks or suspicious domains (e.g., hits.dwyl.com) from installation scripts
Presence of redundant exfiltration logic in both preinstall scripts and main entry points (e.g., new.js and index.js)
file_indicators: package.json with preinstall field referencing suspicious scripts such as new.js
new.js or index.js files containing combined use of os, https, and child_process modules for data collection and transmission
Hardcoded references to external domains such as discord.com/api/webhooks or hits.dwyl.com in JavaScript files
network_indicators: Outbound HTTPS POST requests to hits.dwyl.com/api/collect
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor npm package installations for preinstall scripts that access system information (username, hostname, public IP) and initiate outbound network requests to external domains, especially Discord webhooks or non-standard endpoints like hits.dwyl.com. Flag packages with suspiciously named scripts (e.g., new.js) referenced in package.json preinstall fields. Use static analysis to detect the use of os, https, and child_process modules in installation or entry-point scripts, and employ network monitoring to identify exfiltration attempts to known malicious endpoints. Pay special attention to packages with names mimicking popular libraries, as these are common in typosquatting campaigns.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code executes a bundled credential recovery tool (WebBrowserPassView) using child_process.exec, extracts browser-stored credentials to an HTML file, reads the file contents, sends the data via HTTP POST to a hardcoded external server, and deletes the output file to remove evidence.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code launches an external credential recovery tool to harvest sensitive browser credentials, exfiltrates the data to an attacker-controlled server, and deletes the evidence. This sequence is characteristic of credential-stealing malware and is highly suspicious in any npm package.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate npm packages do not execute external binaries, harvest user credentials, or communicate with unknown external servers. They also do not perform anti-forensic actions such as deleting evidence files after exfiltration.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Password recovery tools like WebBrowserPassView may be used by end-users for local credential recovery, but never as part of an npm package or with automated exfiltration to a remote server.
key_indicators: Execution of WebBrowserPassView or similar credential recovery binaries from within the package
Automated reading and exfiltration of credential data files (e.g., out.html)
Outbound HTTP POST requests to hardcoded, suspicious domains (e.g., 1.host.jwte.ch:1337/pwn)
Immediate deletion of output files after exfiltration (anti-forensics)

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when the package is executed as part of a build process or script execution)
execution_context.file_location: main JavaScript file of bb-builder package (e.g., index.js or main entry point)

package_info.why_malicious: The package embeds and executes a credential-stealing binary (WebBrowserPassView) to extract browser-stored credentials, exfiltrates the stolen data to an external attacker-controlled server, and deletes evidence of the theft. The malicious code is intentionally obfuscated within a seemingly legitimate npm package, and such behavior is never expected in any legitimate npm package.

attack_chain.action: User installs or executes the bb-builder package, which triggers the malicious JavaScript code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Execution of credential recovery tool

attack_chain.action: The package executes the bundled WebBrowserPassView binary to extract browser-stored credentials and saves them to an HTML file (out.html).
attack_chain.leads_to: Credential data is written to disk

attack_chain.action: The package reads the credential data from the HTML file and sends it via HTTP POST to the attacker's server at http://1.host.jwte.ch:1337/pwn.
attack_chain.leads_to: Exfiltration of sensitive credentials

attack_chain.action: The package deletes the HTML file containing the credentials to remove evidence of the theft.
attack_chain.leads_to: Anti-forensics; attack complete

behavioral_signatures: Execution of external credential recovery tools (e.g., WebBrowserPassView) from within npm package scripts
Automated creation and deletion of temporary credential data files (e.g., out.html) during package execution
Outbound HTTP POST requests to hardcoded, suspicious domains during package runtime
Immediate removal of files containing sensitive data after network exfiltration
file_indicators: Presence of WebBrowserPassView or similar binaries (e.g., extension.exe) in npm package directories (e.g., node_modules/bb-builder/)
Creation and subsequent deletion of files named out.html or similar in the working directory
Suspicious executable files bundled within JavaScript packages
network_indicators: HTTP POST requests to http://1.host.jwte.ch:1337/pwn or similar credential collection endpoints
Outbound network connections from npm package scripts to unknown or untrusted domains
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for npm packages that bundle and execute credential recovery tools such as WebBrowserPassView, especially those that create and quickly delete temporary files containing credentials. Flag any package that makes HTTP POST requests to hardcoded or suspicious domains (e.g., 1.host.jwte.ch:1337) during installation or runtime. Use static analysis to detect embedded binaries and dynamic analysis to observe file creation/deletion and network activity during package execution.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time or runtime, the code defines an array of hardcoded URLs pointing to malicious Windows executables hosted on a non-official GitHub repository, preparing for subsequent download and execution of infostealer malware.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The presence of hardcoded URLs to external .exe files, especially from an untrusted GitHub repository, is a strong indicator of malware staging. The URLs directly reference known infostealer payloads.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate npm packages should never reference or prepare to download executables from untrusted or unofficial sources, nor should they include links to known malware.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate updaters or installers may reference official binaries for updates, but only from trusted, verified sources and with user awareness.
key_indicators: Hardcoded external URLs to .exe files in JavaScript source
References to known malware (Skuld Infostealer, Blank Grabber)
Use of GitHub as a malware hosting platform
Obfuscated or minified code to hide intent

execution_context.trigger: At import-time or runtime (when the package is installed or imported by a project)
execution_context.file_location: Main entry JavaScript file (e.g., index.js or main.js) of the malicious npm package

package_info.why_malicious: These packages are typosquatted variants of popular Roblox developer modules. They contain obfuscated JavaScript that, upon installation or import, downloads and executes infostealer malware (Skuld and Blank Grabber) from external sources. The code enables remote code execution, exfiltration of sensitive data, and poses severe risks to users by compromising credentials and system integrity.

attack_chain.action: User installs or imports the malicious npm package, triggering execution of the main JavaScript file.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is loaded and begins execution.

attack_chain.action: Malicious code defines URLs to malware executables hosted on GitHub.
attack_chain.leads_to: Preparation for malware download.

attack_chain.action: The downloadAndRun function is invoked, downloading the malware executables to the victim's system using PowerShell.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malware binaries are present on the victim's machine.

attack_chain.action: The downloaded executables (Skuld Infostealer and Blank Grabber) are executed, compromising the system.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malware runs, stealing credentials and sensitive data.

attack_chain.action: Stolen data is exfiltrated to the threat actor via Discord webhooks or Telegram.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives sensitive information; compromise complete.

behavioral_signatures: npm package executes PowerShell commands at install or import time to download and run external executables
Download and execution of Windows executables from non-official GitHub repositories within npm package code
Obfuscated or minified JavaScript that references external URLs for .exe files
Automated invocation of exec/execAsync with PowerShell download and execution logic
file_indicators: Presence of hardcoded URLs to github.com/zvydev/code/raw/main/*.exe in JavaScript source
References to RobloxPlayerLauncher.exe and cmd.exe in package code
Obfuscated or minified JavaScript in main entry files (index.js, main.js) of npm packages
network_indicators: Potential connections to Telegram APIs for data exfiltration
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor npm package installations and imports for execution of PowerShell or shell commands that download and run external executables, especially from non-official sources. Flag packages containing hardcoded URLs to suspicious GitHub repositories or .exe files. Use static analysis to detect obfuscated JavaScript that invokes exec/execAsync with download and execution logic. Monitor for outbound connections to known C2 channels such as Discord webhooks and Telegram APIs. Identify packages with references to known malware filenames or suspicious network destinations in their code.

matched_knowledge.source_package: Unknown (Jade Sleet & Moonstone Sleet campaigns, multiple packages) (npm)

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At import-time or runtime, the code reads a token from a file in a hidden directory, sends it via HTTPS POST to a hardcoded remote server, writes the server's response as a new JavaScript file, and immediately executes it as a child process, resulting in exfiltration of local data and arbitrary remote code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code chains together reading a local secret, exfiltrating it to a suspicious domain, downloading a new script, and executing it, all without user knowledge or consent. It disables TLS certificate validation, further increasing risk.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal packages do not exfiltrate local data or execute downloaded code automatically, nor do they disable TLS certificate validation.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Automated updaters may download and run code, but only with explicit user consent, from trusted sources, and with proper TLS validation.
key_indicators: Reading secret from hidden directory
POSTing data to hardcoded suspicious domain
Writing and executing remote code as a new file
Disabling TLS certificate validation

package_info.package_name: Unknown (Jade Sleet & Moonstone Sleet campaigns, multiple packages)
package_info.package_versions: Multiple versions, published between Summer 2023 and Q2 2024
package_info.why_malicious: These packages are designed to execute arbitrary code on installation or import, exfiltrate data, download and execute additional payloads, and target both Windows and Linux systems. They use obfuscation, multi-stage payloads, and anti-forensics to evade detection and maximize impact.

attack_chain.action: Initial package creates hidden directory and fetches remote data, storing it locally.
attack_chain.leads_to: Preparation for further malicious activity by second package.

attack_chain.action: Second package reads local token, exfiltrates it, downloads and executes new malicious code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Arbitrary code execution and further compromise.

attack_chain.action: Single-package variant (Moonstone Sleet) downloads, decrypts, and executes remote payload on Windows, then deletes evidence.
attack_chain.leads_to: Immediate compromise and anti-forensics.

attack_chain.action: Linux-targeting variant sets up directory, installs and runs disguised binary, deletes installer script.
attack_chain.leads_to: Persistence and stealthy execution on Linux systems.

behavioral_signatures: Creation of hidden or misleadingly named directories in user home or application support paths (e.g., .svnlook, ~/Library/Application Support/UpdateProvider)
Synchronous or asynchronous network requests to hardcoded suspicious domains or IPs during install/import
Writing and executing files downloaded from remote servers, especially as new scripts or binaries
Immediate deletion of installer or script files after execution (anti-forensics)
Conditional OS-specific payload execution (e.g., Windows vs Linux branches)
Disabling TLS certificate validation in Node.js environment
file_indicators: svntoken, checksvn.js, preinstall.bat, preinstall.ps1, sqlite.a, updateMacOS
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for creation of hidden or misleadingly named directories and files in user home or application support paths, unexpected network requests to known malicious domains or IPs during install/import, execution of downloaded scripts or binaries, and immediate file deletion post-install. Flag packages that conditionally execute OS-specific payloads, disable TLS certificate validation, or use obfuscated/encoded payloads. Correlate with known IOCs and behavioral patterns from Jade Sleet and Moonstone Sleet campaigns for high-confidence detection.

matched_knowledge.source_package: TeamViewer.exe / BetterShaders Setup 1.0.3.exe / Software.exe (malicious Electron apps) (NSIS installer (Electron app distribution))

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime (upon application execution), the code collects system information, browser history, and credentials from the filesystem using Node.js APIs, then sends this data via an outbound HTTP POST request to the gofile.io file-sharing service, resulting in exfiltration of sensitive user data to an external attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code programmatically accesses sensitive files such as browser history and credential stores, then transmits this data to an external file-sharing service (gofile.io) without user knowledge or consent. This behavior is characteristic of infostealer malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Electron applications should not access or transmit user credentials, browser history, or detailed system information without explicit user consent and clear disclosure. Accessing and exfiltrating such data is a direct violation of user privacy and security expectations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate applications may collect anonymized telemetry or crash logs, but they do not access credential stores or browser histories, and always request user consent for any data collection or transmission.
key_indicators: Direct file access to browser history and credential files from within Electron app resources
Outbound HTTP POST requests to gofile.io/upload or similar file-sharing endpoints
Node.js code embedded in .asar archives performing OS-level data harvesting
Absence of user prompts or consent dialogs for sensitive data access or transmission

required_permissions: filesystem (read access to browser and credential files)

package_info.package_name: TeamViewer.exe / BetterShaders Setup 1.0.3.exe / Software.exe (malicious Electron apps)
package_info.why_malicious: These packages are Electron-based desktop applications distributed via NSIS installers that contain malicious Node.js code within their .asar archives. The code is designed to harvest sensitive user data, including system information, browser histories, and credentials, and exfiltrate it to external file-sharing services such as gofile.io. The applications masquerade as legitimate software to evade detection and facilitate data theft.

attack_chain.action: User downloads and executes a trojanized Electron app distributed as an NSIS installer.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious Electron app is installed and launched.

attack_chain.action: Electron app unpacks and executes Node.js code from the .asar archive (a.js) upon application startup.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is loaded into memory and prepared for execution.

attack_chain.action: Malicious Node.js code collects system information, browser history, and credentials from the victim's machine.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive data is gathered from the victim's machine.

attack_chain.action: Collected data is exfiltrated to gofile.io via HTTP POST request.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives stolen data via the file-sharing service.

behavioral_signatures: Electron app accessing browser history and credential files without user consent
Electron app making outbound HTTP POST requests to file-sharing services such as gofile.io
Node.js code within .asar archives performing OS-level data collection and exfiltration
file_indicators: Presence of suspicious .asar files in Electron app resources (e.g., app\resources\app.asar\a.js)
NSIS installer files with hashes: 9926e2782d603061b52d88f83d93e7af, cfc6e0014b3cc8d4dcaf0d76e2382556, b150afa6b3642ea1da1233b76f7b454e
network_indicators: Outbound connections to https://gofile.io/upload from Electron app processes
Unusual HTTP POST requests containing system or credential data to file-sharing domains
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor Electron-based applications for unauthorized access to sensitive files such as browser history and credential stores. Inspect .asar archives for embedded Node.js scripts that perform data harvesting or exfiltration. Flag NSIS installers with known malicious hashes or those that unpack Electron apps exhibiting these behaviors. Monitor network traffic for outbound HTTP POST requests to gofile.io/upload or similar file-sharing services originating from Electron app processes.
